entries.name: Hugh Edmundson v. Theorem Technology, Inc.

arguments_rejected_or_waived: Company's argument that the disputed § 5.17(b) language is merely a "scoping device": rejected; even so, the scope of Edmundson's post-termination obligations is expressly tied to his past activities as an officer and director, making the claim "inextricably intertwined" with his corporate role.

Company's argument that the agreement-wide definition of "client" (all investors in funds managed or advised by the Company Group) applies, so no prior relationship with Edmundson is required: rejected (fn. 5) because it would render the specific "[f]or purposes of this Section 5.17(b)" definition surplusage and the specific provision controls the general.

Company's argument, raised in a reply-brief footnote, that advancement is not warranted for the § 5.17(b)(iii) claim: not considered because it was absent from the Opening Brief and not fairly presented to the Magistrate (fn. 7).

Company's argument that a counterclaim must do more than merely produce a damages award to "offset" a claim: rejected; although the Court recognized the concern (shared by Zaman) that otherwise the two Roven prongs collapse for damages counterclaims, the broad reading of "offset" forecloses requiring that the counterclaim entirely defeat the affirmative claim.
Company's remaining arguments that advancement is not warranted to defend its affirmative claims: rejected as answered by the Report's reasoning (Report ¶¶ 12–14).

authorities_cited.authority: Citadel Hldg. Corp. v. Roven, 603 A.2d 818 (Del. 1992)
authorities_cited.proposition: Counterclaim expenses are advanceable if the counterclaim is compulsory and "advanced to defeat, or offset" an affirmative claim the official is entitled to advancement to defend.

authorities_cited.authority: Pontone v. Milso Indus. Corp., 2014 WL 2439973 (Del. Ch. May 29, 2014) (Pontone I)
authorities_cited.proposition: Reading Zaman to exclude compulsory counterclaims that offset but cannot defeat affirmative claims conflicts with Roven, which controls; a counterclaim need not entirely defeat the claim.

authorities_cited.authority: Pontone v. Milso Indus. Corp., 100 A.3d 1023 (Del. Ch. 2014) (Pontone II)
authorities_cited.proposition: "Inextricably intertwined" standard for connecting claims to the official's corporate capacity.

authorities_cited.authority: Merger Agreement § 5.17(b)
authorities_cited.proposition: Restrictive covenant's "customer or client" definition ties post-termination obligations to Edmundson's pre-closing contacts and responsibilities as officer and director.

authorities_cited.authority: Barr v. Genesis CMG Hldgs., LLC, 2025 WL 3720720 (Del. Ch. Dec. 23, 2025)
authorities_cited.proposition: Solicitation allegations concerning clients the plaintiff learned of through his official capacity are inextricably intertwined with his former position.

authorities_cited.authority: Charney v. Am. Apparel, Inc., 2015 WL 5313769 (Del. Ch. Sept. 11, 2015)
authorities_cited.proposition: No advancement for defending standstill-breach claim arising from proxy contest initiated as an individual with no use or abuse of corporate power or alleged misuse of company information; here the covenant language and alleged use of Company information connect the claim to corporate status.

authorities_cited.authority: Krauss v. 180 Life Scis. Corp., 2022 WL 665323 (Del. Ch. Mar. 7, 2022)
authorities_cited.proposition: "Offset" in Roven is construed broadly.

authorities_cited.authority: Transamerica Occidental Life Ins. Co. v. Aviation Off. of Am., Inc., 292 F.3d 384 (3d Cir. 2002)
authorities_cited.proposition: "Logical relationship" test for compulsory counterclaims.

authorities_cited.authority: Rogers v. Mary Kay Hldg. Corp., 2025 WL 3199166 (Del. Ch. Nov. 17, 2025)
authorities_cited.proposition: Close advancement questions should be resolved in favor of advancement given Delaware policy of assuring litigation expense protection for fiduciaries.

authorities_cited.authority: Sunline Com. Carriers, Inc. v. CITGO Petrol. Corp., 206 A.3d 836 (Del. 2019)
authorities_cited.proposition: Contracts are read to give each provision effect and avoid surplusage.

authorities_cited.authority: Crispo v. Musk, 304 A.3d 567 (Del. Ch. 2023)
authorities_cited.proposition: Specific contract language controls over general language.

authorities_cited.authority: Emerald P'rs v. Berlin, 726 A.2d 1215 (Del. 1999)
authorities_cited.proposition: Arguments not raised in the opening brief are not considered.

authorities_cited.authority: Bronstein v. Tyson 2.0, Inc., 2026 WL 3182483 (Del. Ch. Oct. 23, 2026)
authorities_cited.proposition: "[T]he exceptions process is not available for parties to spring new arguments."

authorities_cited.authority: Zaman v. Amedeo Hldgs., Inc., 2008 WL 2168397 (Del. Ch.)
authorities_cited.proposition: Advanceable counterclaims require a tight nexus akin to affirmative defenses; read narrowly to the extent it conflicts with Roven's "offset" language.

authorities_cited.authority: DiGiacobbe v. Sestak, 743 A.2d 180 (Del. 1999)
authorities_cited.proposition: De novo review of a Magistrate's report on exceptions.

authorities_cited.authority: Kaung v. Cole Nat'l Corp., 884 A.2d 500 (Del. 2005)
authorities_cited.proposition: Arguments may be re-raised in a later indemnification or recoupment proceeding.

authorities_cited.authority: White v. Curo Tex. Hldgs., LLC, 2017 WL 1369332 (Del. Ch. Feb. 21, 2017)
authorities_cited.proposition: Deferring less clear-cut disputes to the indemnification stage avoids excessive advancement litigation.

authorities_cited.authority: Bowers v. Black Lives Matter Glob. Network Found., Inc., 2026 WL 2023082 (Del. Ch. July 13, 2026)
authorities_cited.proposition: Where some entitlement is shown but scope is ambiguous, grant advancement and defer disputes to indemnification.

summary.brief_summary: Hugh Edmundson, Theorem Technology, Inc.'s co-founder and former director and officer, sought advancement for defending and counterclaiming in an ICC arbitration alleging he breached a Merger Agreement restrictive covenant; a Magistrate ruled largely in his favor on cross-motions for summary judgment, and the Company took exceptions. Vice Chancellor Cook overruled the exceptions on de novo review, holding the covenant claim intertwined with his corporate capacity because § 5.17(b) defines covered customers by his pre-closing contacts and responsibilities and the Company contends he misused Company information. The Court also held that the compulsory counterclaim's costs are advanceable under Roven's broadly read "offset" prong because success would partly impair the Company's claim, resolving that close question in favor of advancement.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether a former director and officer is entitled to advancement for (i) defending an ICC arbitration claim that he breached a Merger Agreement restrictive covenant (§ 5.17(b)) whose "customer or client" definition turns on his contacts and responsibilities during the twelve months before closing, and (ii) prosecuting a breach-of-contract counterclaim that, if successful, would only partly impair rather than wholly defeat the Company's claim, under Citadel Holding Corp. v. Roven's "defeat, or offset" test.

flags.evidence: True, as the Company mentions, the disputed language in § 5.17(b) operates as a “scoping device.” But the scope of Edmundson’s ongoing post-termination obligations... is expressly tied to his past activities
flags.opinion_says: The Court accepts the Company's point that the language is a scoping device but holds the scope is nonetheless tied to his past activities as officer and director.
flags.problem: The Court conceded the language is a scoping device rather than rejecting that argument; it rejected the inference that this avoids the intertwining.

flags.assertion: Every exception argument must be raised before the Magistrate and in the opening exceptions brief; a reply-brief footnote will not preserve it.
flags.evidence: This argument did not feature in the Company’s Opening Brief, nor does it appear to have been fairly presented to the Magistrate. I decline to consider it now.
flags.opinion_says: The Court declined one specific argument raised only in a reply footnote and not fairly presented to the Magistrate; it did not announce a rule that every argument must be raised both places.
flags.problem: The Court only declined one argument absent from the opening brief and apparently not presented to the Magistrate, and did not hold both requirements are always necessary.

summary.holding: After de novo review, the Court overruled the Company's exceptions and adopted the Magistrate's Report as an order of the Court, subject to a clarification of the counterclaim analysis. On defense of the Company's § 5.17(b)(i) claim, the Court held the claim inextricably intertwined with Edmundson's role as director and officer because the covenant's "customer or client" definition is expressly tied to his pre-closing contacts and responsibilities, following Barr and distinguishing Charney because here the Company contends Edmundson improperly used Company information; the arbitration statement of claim's suggestion that he shared confidential information learned during his tenure provides an independent basis. The § 5.17(b)(iii) argument was not considered as first raised in a reply footnote. On the breach-of-contract counterclaim, the Court agreed it is compulsory under the logical-relationship test, and clarified the second Roven prong: following Pontone I and Krauss, "offset" is read broadly, so a counterclaim need not be capable of entirely defeating the affirmative claim; because success would at least in part impair the Company's damages claim, it qualifies. Acknowledging the question is less clear-cut, the Court resolved it in favor of advancement, noting (fn. 27) that the Company may re-raise its arguments in a plenary indemnification or recoupment proceeding.
key_facts_and_concessions: Merger Agreement § 5.17(b) defines "customer or client" as someone with whom Edmundson "had contact" or "for whose relationship with the Company Group" he was responsible "during the twelve (12) months before the merger's closing."
The Certificate of Incorporation and Indemnification Agreement together grant Edmundson a mandatory advancement right with the maximum scope permissible under Delaware law (fn. 1).

Theorem's arbitration statement of claim alleges that Edmundson, after being "terminated over the weekend," emailed a Theorem investor that he could now "speak freely," and that investors then demanded liquidating trusts (fn. 14); the Court found it apparent that Theorem contends Edmundson improperly used Company information.

Edmundson's counterclaim alleges Pagaya damaged relationships with Theorem investors through "unlawful meddling in violation of the Merger Agreement," challenging the exact conduct he is alleged to have disclosed in violation of the covenant.
Edmundson is the co-founder and a former director and officer of Theorem Technology, Inc. (the "Company"); the ICC arbitration arises from the Company's sale to Pagaya Technologies Ltd.
On cross-motions for summary judgment, the Magistrate's September 14, 2026 Report ruled "for the most part" in Edmundson's favor; the Company took exceptions.
Edmundson recognized at oral argument that the Company could re-raise many of its arguments in a plenary indemnification or recoupment proceeding (fn. 27).
summary.practical_takeaway: Companies resisting advancement for covenant claims should expect that covenants scoped by reference to the executive's pre-closing contacts or responsibilities, coupled with allegations of misuse of company information, will be treated as arising from corporate capacity, and that compulsory counterclaims that could even partly offset the company's claim will be advanceable. Every exception argument must be raised before the Magistrate and in the opening exceptions brief; a reply-brief footnote will not preserve it.
summary.standard_of_review: De novo review by a constitutional judge of a Magistrate's final report on exceptions (DiGiacobbe v. Sestak).

entries.name: George Assad v. Carine S. Clark, et al.

arguments_rejected_or_waived: Defendants' reading that § 4 is only an "equal treatment provision" governing distributions "if and when the Company determines to make a distribution": rejected as unreasonable. Section 4 lacks § 2.1's "when, as and if declared by the Board" qualifier. Defendants' reading would make § 4 largely repeat § 2.1. Section 4 also stands alone as "Liquidation Rights" rather than under § 2, "Identical Rights" (fn. 3).
Defendants' argument that Plaintiff seeks nothing more than a dividend: turned against them, because under their reading § 4 would then do no additional work (fn. 3).

Defendants' argument that a mandatory distribution would "serve no conceivable commercial purpose" and that unhappy stockholders can sell: rejected. Mandating a distribution that stops the Company from investing in an entirely new sector is not irrational. The shares trade below cash held, and Defendants' outcome (a cash-and-NOL shell with no business plan) is equally strange.

Defendants' argument that Plaintiff's reading yields irrational results in other Liquidation Events (e.g., a stock-for-stock merger leaving the Company with a minority stake): rejected. Hypotheticals do not make the plain reading unreasonable, and, as Plaintiff argued, the Company could amend the Charter or forgo such a transaction.

Defendants' argument that § 4 cannot require distribution of all net cash before providing for claims under DGCL Section 281: rejected. Section 4 reaches only assets "legally available for distribution," and Defendants did not explain any conflict with Section 281. Determining what is legally available is for the Board in the first instance.

Defendants' laches argument that Plaintiff should have sued after the July 22 announcement: rejected. It was reasonable to wait until the sale closed and proceeds were actually withheld, and suit came two days after closing. Defendants' authorities involved longer delays in suits seeking to enjoin transactions, whereas Plaintiff does not challenge the Asset Sale.

Defendants' laches prejudice argument that earlier suit would have allowed alternative transactions or structures valuing the NOLs: rejected. The Board and majority holders had approved the sale before announcement, the consent eliminated termination rights, and the forbearance deadline was nine days away. Defendants were also on notice of their own Charter.
Plaintiff's reliance on other companies' charters and Defendants' response that "market precedent" is irrelevant: not reached because the Charter is unambiguous (fn. 7).

authorities_cited.authority: Huckleberry.ai Charter art. V, §§ 1.3, 1.10, 2, 2.1, 4
authorities_cited.proposition: A Liquidation Event includes an Asset Transfer. Section 4 mandates that legally available assets "shall be distributed," in contrast to § 2.1's board-discretionary dividend language.

authorities_cited.authority: Alta Berkeley VI C.V. v. Omneon, Inc., 41 A.3d 381 (Del. 2012)
authorities_cited.proposition: Charters are contracts between the corporation and its stockholders; a term is ambiguous only if fairly or reasonably susceptible to more than one meaning.

authorities_cited.authority: Osborn ex rel. Osborn v. Kemp, 991 A.2d 1153 (Del. 2010)
authorities_cited.proposition: Clear and unambiguous contract terms are given their plain meaning.

authorities_cited.authority: Williams Cos., Inc. v. Energy Transfer LP, 2020 WL 3581095 (Del. Ch. July 2, 2020)
authorities_cited.proposition: Different language in different sections suggests an intended difference in meaning.

authorities_cited.authority: O'Brien v. Progressive N. Ins. Co., 785 A.2d 281 (Del. 2001)
authorities_cited.proposition: Interpretations giving effect to each term are preferred over readings that make terms uselessly repetitive.

authorities_cited.authority: West Willow-Bay Ct., LLC v. Robino-Bay Ct. Plaza, LLC, 2007 WL 3317551 (Del. Ch. Nov. 2, 2007)
authorities_cited.proposition: Courts avoid constructions that render terms repetitive or surplusage.

authorities_cited.authority: Zurich Am. Ins. Co. v. St. Paul Surplus Lines, Inc., 2009 WL 4895120 (Del. Ch. Dec. 10, 2009)
authorities_cited.proposition: "Shall" makes an act mandatory.

authorities_cited.authority: Bergonzi v. Rite Aid Corp., 2003 WL 22407303 (Del. Ch. Oct. 20, 2003)
authorities_cited.proposition: Contra proferentem: ambiguity in a charter is construed against the corporation.

authorities_cited.authority: Bank of New York Mellon v. Commerzbank Cap. Funding Tr. II, 65 A.3d 539 (Del. 2013)
authorities_cited.proposition: Contracts creating rights in public securities investors are read to give effect to investors' reasonable expectations.

authorities_cited.authority: Quill v. Malizia, 2005 WL 578975 (Del. Ch. Mar. 4, 2005)
authorities_cited.proposition: Laches requires prejudice from unreasonable delay after at least inquiry notice.

authorities_cited.authority: Gradient OC Master, Ltd. v. NBC Universal, Inc., 930 A.2d 104 (Del. Ch. 2007)
authorities_cited.proposition: It is not unreasonable to wait until certain a transaction will proceed before suing.

authorities_cited.authority: Deputy v. Deputy, 2020 WL 1018554 (Del. Ch. Mar. 2, 2020)
authorities_cited.proposition: There is no laches prejudice where defendants could not reasonably have been unaware of possible future claims (quoting Stewart v. Wilm. Tr. SP Servs., Inc., 112 A.3d 271 (Del. Ch. 2015)).

authorities_cited.authority: Bacine v. Scharffenberger, 1984 WL 21128 (Del. Ch. Dec. 11, 1984)
authorities_cited.proposition: Laches for delay in suing to prevent consummation of a transaction; inapplicable because Plaintiff challenges only the withholding of proceeds.
Summary judgment standard; cross-motions without a material fact dispute may be deemed a stipulation for decision on the record.

authorities_cited.authority: XO Commc'ns, LLC v. Level 3 Commc'ns, Inc., 948 A.2d 1111 (Del. Ch. 2007)
authorities_cited.proposition: Summary judgment is appropriate for an unambiguous contract.

authorities_cited.authority: Baring v. Condrell, 2004 WL 2340047 (Del. Ch. Oct. 18, 2004)
authorities_cited.proposition: The same standard applies to each cross-motion.

authorities_cited.authority: Kaiser Aluminum Corp. v. Matheson, 681 A.2d 392 (Del. 1996)
authorities_cited.proposition: Governing documents are interpreted under contract principles.

authorities_cited.authority: Kuhn Constr., Inc. v. Diamond State Port Corp., 990 A.2d 393 (Del. 2010)
authorities_cited.proposition: A contract is read as a whole, avoiding surplusage.

authorities_cited.authority: Rhone-Poulenc Basic Chems. Co. v. Am. Motorists Ins. Co., 616 A.2d 1192 (Del. 1992)
authorities_cited.proposition: Disagreement over construction does not create ambiguity.

authorities_cited.authority: City Investing Co. Liquidating Tr. v. Cont'l Cas. Co., 624 A.2d 1191 (Del. 1993)
authorities_cited.proposition: A plain writing is the sole source of intent.

authorities_cited.authority: GC Broadway, LLC v. AN SM 1925 Broadway Hldgs., LLC, 2026 WL 539233 (Del. Ch. Feb. 26, 2026); Pacira BioSciences, Inc. v. Fortis Advisors LLC, 2021 WL 4949179 (Del. Ch. Oct. 25, 2021); Deluxe Ent. Servs. Inc. v. DLX Acq. Corp., 2021 WL 1169905 (Del. Ch. Mar. 29, 2021); Hampton v. Turner, 2015 WL 1947067 (Del. Ch. Apr. 29, 2015); MicroStrategy Inc. v. Acacia Rsch. Corp., 2010 WL 5550455 (Del. Ch. Dec. 30, 2010)
authorities_cited.proposition: Parties who use different language elsewhere show they knew how to say something when they intended it (fn. 2).

authorities_cited.authority: Whittington v. Dragon Grp., L.L.C., 991 A.2d 1 (Del. 2009)
authorities_cited.proposition: Laches rests on the maxim that equity aids the vigilant.
Stipulated that the Asset Sale is a sale of all or substantially all assets under § 271.
Defendants' argument that a mandatory distribution conflicts with claim-provision requirements; the Court found no conflict explained.

summary.brief_summary: Class B stockholder George Assad sued Huckleberry.ai, Inc. (f/k/a Domo, Inc.) and its directors after the Company sold substantially all its assets to Progress for about $400 million (netting about $221 million) and announced it would not liquidate but would redeploy the cash to monetize its NOLs. On expedited cross-motions for summary judgment directed to a stipulated question, Vice Chancellor David held that the Charter's Liquidation Rights provision, triggered by the stipulated Asset Transfer, mandates distribution of legally available assets. The Court reasoned from the contrast with the board-discretionary dividend clause and the anti-surplusage canon, with contra proferentem as a fallback. The Court also rejected Defendants' laches defense for lack of both unreasonable delay and prejudice.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether Article V, Section 4 of the Charter, which provides that "[i]n the event of a Liquidation Event" (defined to include an "Asset Transfer" of all or substantially all assets) "the assets of the Corporation legally available for distribution to stockholders shall be distributed" pro rata to common holders, mandates a distribution after a controller-approved sale of substantially all assets, or merely governs equal treatment if and when the Board elects to distribute; and whether laches bars the claim.

flags.assertion: After the Asset Sale, the Company announced and stated in its Information Statement
flags.evidence: The same day, the Company publicly announced that it had entered into the APA... “The Company does not intend to liquidate following the Closing.”
flags.opinion_says: The non-liquidation statement was made in the July 22 announcement and the August 24 Information Statement, both before the September 22 closing.
flags.problem: The announcement and Information Statement came before the closing (July 22 and August 24), not after the Asset Sale.

summary.holding: On the stipulated question, the Court held that the Asset Sale obligates the Company to distribute all legally available assets under Charter art. V, § 4. Section 4 unambiguously mandates distribution in a Liquidation Event: "shall" is mandatory, § 4 lacks § 2.1's board-discretion language, and Defendants' equal-treatment reading would make § 4 surplusage. Even if Defendants' reading were reasonable, contra proferentem would resolve the ambiguity against the corporation, so Plaintiff's reading controls either way. What assets are "legally available for distribution" is for the Board to determine in the first instance; the parties agree the NOLs are not distributable. Laches does not apply. Suing two days after closing was not unreasonable delay, because Plaintiff challenges the withholding of proceeds, not the sale. There was no prejudice, because the sale was locked up by Board and majority approval and the forbearance deadline, and Defendants were on notice of their own Charter. The opinion resolves the Cross-Motions on the stipulated issue in Plaintiff's favor. It does not separately state the grant or denial of each motion, address Count II, order relief, or set follow-up deadlines.
key_facts_and_concessions: The parties stipulated that the Asset Sale is a sale of "all or substantially all" of the Company's assets under DGCL Section 271. It is therefore an "Asset Transfer" (Charter art. V, § 1.3) and a "Liquidation Event" (§ 1.10).
Charter art. V, § 4 states that legally available assets "shall be distributed" in a Liquidation Event. By contrast, § 2.1 entitles holders to dividends only "when, as and if declared by the Board."

After the Asset Sale, the Company announced and stated in its Information Statement that it "does not intend to liquidate." The Board would instead evaluate uses of the proceeds, including acquisitions "without limitation as to industry"; stockholders would not receive proceeds.

The Asset Sale to Progress Software Corporation was approved by the Board and by written consent of James and Cocolalla, LLC (75.7% of voting power through the Class A stock). That consent, delivered within one hour of signing, eliminated the Company's ability to terminate the APA.

The Company received about $221 million at the September 22, 2026 closing after debt repayment. It retained over $900 million of NOLs and no other material non-cash assets, and it is bound by a three-year non-compete (fn. 5).
The parties agree the NOLs are not available for distribution (fn. 6). Defendants acknowledged that net cash per share exceeds the trading price (fn. 4).

Timeline: announcement July 22, 2026; Information Statement August 24; closing September 22; suit filed September 24. The forbearance agreement required a definitive agreement by July 31, failing which the Company would likely need to file for bankruptcy.
Plaintiff moved only on Count I; Defendants moved on Counts I and II (fn. 1).
summary.practical_takeaway: Companies whose charters define "Liquidation Event" to include asset transfers and say legally available assets "shall be distributed" should treat that clause as a mandatory payout. Before closing a sale meant to redeploy cash, they should amend the Charter, as the Court noted the Company could, rather than rely on board discretion. Stockholders challenging only the post-closing withholding of proceeds can wait until the sale closes and the proceeds are actually withheld without risking laches.
summary.standard_of_review: Ct. Ch. R. 56(a) summary judgment on cross-motions directed to a stipulated question (Dkt. 15). The Court noted that under Rule 56(i) it may deem cross-motions with no material factual dispute a stipulation for decision on the record, and that summary judgment suits an unambiguous contract. Unambiguous charter terms are given their plain meaning; any ambiguity in a charter is construed against the corporation (contra proferentem).
